 A Republican senator pushing an ambitious $1.5 trillion plan to shore up Social Security says Donald Trump has personally committed to backing the legislation, but experts told Newsweek that it's not a perfect plan. Senator Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana Republican, told Face the Nation on Sunday that his proposal would establish an investment fund separate from Social Security's existing trust funds, using borrowed federal money that would be invested in the broader economy for decades. According to Cassidy, the investment gains could eventually cover as much as 70 percent of Social Security's unfunded obligations. “The president actually has given me personal commitment that he would support it, and his administration has been very helpful,” Cassidy said. “I have Democrats who are also supportive. It's a bipartisan bill.” The proposal comes as lawmakers face growing pressure to address Social Security's finances. Currently, the 2026 trustees' projections indicate the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund will only be able to pay full scheduled benefits until the fourth quarter of 2032. At that point, the continuing income would cover just 78 percent of scheduled benefits. Why It Matters Social Security provides a financial lifeline to tens of millions of retirees and people with disabilities. Cassidy has previously warned that lawmakers should address the financing problem before the fund’s insolvency forces Congress into more difficult decisions involving taxes or lower benefits. Now Cassidy said he believes there is a path to 60 votes in the Senate, House passage as well as a presidential signature, though no such outcome is yet assured. What the $1.5 Trillion Social Security Proposal Would Do Cassidy's proposal would significantly change how the federal government would attempt to finance part of Social Security's long-term obligations. Rather than putting the money directly into the existing Social Security trust funds, the government would borrow $1.5 trillion and establish a separate investment fund. Cassidy has previously described building up the fund over five years, with roughly $250 billion contributed annually. The money would then be invested in the broader economy, including higher-return assets rather than relying solely on the special Treasury securities traditionally held by Social Security. "We borrow 1.5 trillion dollars, we put it in an investment fund separate from Social Security trust fund, put it into the broader economy, and allow it to grow over six decades," Cassidy told CBS. "At which point it pays for up to 70 percent of what we need to cover the debt for Social Security." Cassidy has also used the federal railroad retirement system as evidence that government retirement assets can be invested in private markets. In Sunday's interview, he argued that Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, had opposed his approach despite previously supporting a similar investment model for railroad retirement. “He doesn't want to put tax dollars in the stock market. He's done that before,” Cassidy said. “He has voted for that exact same policy almost for the federal railroad retirement system under George W. Bush, and that's done fantastic. It works. We know it does.” However, Cassidy’s proposal is not without financial risk. Researchers at the Center for Retirement Research at Boston College have questioned whether investment returns would be sufficiently high and reliable to deliver the results Cassidy has boasted about. In 10,000 simulations run, researchers said the fund failed to repay its borrowing 64 percent of the time under optimistic return assumptions and 83 percent under realistic assumptions. “More borrowing would likely lead to higher deficits and potentially more inflation. The mere idea of borrowing additional money in hopes of generating enough investment returns to offset future liabilities in a pay-as-you-go system seems counter to what is actually needed,” Kevin Thompson, the CEO of 9i Capital Group and the host of the 9innings podcast, told Newsweek. “The entire premise rests on the belief that investment returns will outpace borrowing costs, which is far from guaranteed. You could ultimately push asset prices even higher while transferring additional investment risk onto future taxpayers.” How the Plan Could Affect Social Security Recipients For current beneficiaries, the most important feature of Cassidy's proposal is what it is designed not to do: directly cut promised Social Security benefits. Cassidy has previously said that under his approach, "All risk is borne by the fund; people would get their promised benefits." By generating a new source of financing that could make it easier for the government to continue paying scheduled benefits, Social Security's shortfall wouldn’t exclusively be put on higher payroll taxes or benefit cuts. “The concept of linking Social Security funding to the stock market is nothing new and has been proposed multiple times over the last few decades, as some lawmakers theorized tying that fund to long-term growth could be the answer to the constant concern over Social Security's future viability as a benefits program,” Alex Beene, a financial literacy instructor for the University of Tennessee at Martin, told Newsweek. “At the same time, the Great Recession and subsequent massive decline in the market in 2008 lead to some backing off the idea, as while the long-term trajectory of the market is up, poor performance could generate a firestorm of discussion on Capitol Hill and anger from voters if they feel as if those dollars are suddenly in jeopardy of becoming benefits.” Who Would Be Impacted? The debate around Cassidy’s proposal has implications for both current and future Social Security beneficiaries. For current retirees as well as workers approaching their retirement, they may be able to avoid any potential Social Security cuts once the 2032 funding deadline hits. If Congress did nothing, they’d face a roughly 22 percent cut to benefits otherwise. And for younger workers and future retirees, Cassidy’s plan could be a long-term strategy for protecting the promised benefits they worked and paid for. “Some combination of this idea with others that have been proposed are needed, as more than likely Social Security's future will depend on a combination of factors to maintain benefits for future generations,” Beene said. What Happens Next If Cassidy’s proposal earns the support of enough lawmakers plus Trump, it’s possible that Americans could avoid the costly cuts slated for Social Security just six years from now. Still, there are skeptics of the plan. “If Trump supports the proposal, it certainly improves its political prospects, but congressional approval would still be necessary,” Thompson said. “The goal is to preserve Social Security benefits, but there is no guarantee this strategy will generate the returns necessary to accomplish that.” Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story.
